20: /// A matcher for implementing "word match" semantics.
21: #[derive(Debug)]
22: pub(crate) struct WordMatcher {
23:     /// The regex which is roughly `(?:^|\W)(<original pattern>)(?:$|\W)`.
24:     regex: Regex,
25:     /// The HIR that produced the regex above. We don't keep the HIR for the
26:     /// `original` regex.
27:     ///
28:     /// We put this in an `Arc` because by the time it gets here, it won't
29:     /// change. And because cloning and dropping an `Hir` is somewhat expensive
30:     /// due to its deep recursive representation.
31:     chir: Arc<ConfiguredHIR>,
32:     /// The original regex supplied by the user, which we use in a fast path
33:     /// to try and detect matches before deferring to slower engines.
34:     original: Regex,
35:     /// A map from capture group name to capture group index.
36:     names: HashMap<String, usize>,
37:     /// A thread-safe pool of reusable buffers for finding the match offset of
38:     /// the inner group.
39:     caps: Arc<Pool<Captures, PoolFn>>,
40: }
41: 
42: impl Clone for WordMatcher {
43:     fn clone(&self) -> WordMatcher {
44:         // We implement Clone manually so that we get a fresh Pool such that it
45:         // can set its own thread owner. This permits each thread usings `caps`
46:         // to hit the fast path.
47:         //
48:         // Note that cloning a regex is "cheap" since it uses reference
49:         // counting internally.
50:         let re = self.regex.clone();
51:         WordMatcher {
52:             regex: self.regex.clone(),
53:             chir: Arc::clone(&self.chir),
54:             original: self.original.clone(),
55:             names: self.names.clone(),
56:             caps: Arc::new(Pool::new(Box::new(move || re.create_captures()))),
57:         }
58:     }
59: }
60: 
61: impl WordMatcher {
62:     /// Create a new matcher from the given pattern that only produces matches
63:     /// that are considered "words."
64:     ///
65:     /// The given options are used to construct the regular expression
66:     /// internally.
67:     pub(crate) fn new(chir: ConfiguredHIR) -> Result<WordMatcher, Error> {
68:         let original = chir.clone().into_anchored().to_regex()?;
69:         let chir = Arc::new(chir.into_word()?);
70:         let regex = chir.to_regex()?;
71:         let caps = Arc::new(Pool::new({
72:             let regex = regex.clone();
73:             Box::new(move || regex.create_captures()) as PoolFn
74:         }));
75: 
76:         let mut names = HashMap::new();
77:         let it = regex.group_info().pattern_names(PatternID::ZERO);
78:         for (i, optional_name) in it.enumerate() {
79:             if let Some(name) = optional_name {
80:                 names.insert(name.to_string(), i.checked_sub(1).unwrap());
81:             }
82:         }
83:         Ok(WordMatcher { regex, chir, original, names, caps })
84:     }
85: 
86:     /// Return the underlying regex used to match at word boundaries.
87:     ///
88:     /// The original regex is in the capture group at index 1.
89:     pub(crate) fn regex(&self) -> &Regex {
90:         &self.regex
91:     }
92: 
93:     /// Return the underlying HIR for the regex used to match at word
94:     /// boundaries.
95:     pub(crate) fn chir(&self) -> &ConfiguredHIR {
96:         &self.chir
97:     }
98: 
99:     /// Attempt to do a fast confirmation of a word match that covers a subset
100:     /// (but hopefully a big subset) of most cases. Ok(Some(..)) is returned
101:     /// when a match is found. Ok(None) is returned when there is definitively
102:     /// no match. Err(()) is returned when this routine could not detect
103:     /// whether there was a match or not.
104:     fn fast_find(
105:         &self,
106:         haystack: &[u8],
107:         at: usize,
108:     ) -> Result<Option<Match>, ()> {
109:         // This is a bit hairy. The whole point here is to avoid running a
110:         // slower regex engine to extract capture groups. Remember, our word
111:         // regex looks like this:
112:         //
113:         //     (^|\W)(<original regex>)(\W|$)
114:         //
115:         // What we want are the match offsets of <original regex>. So in the
116:         // easy/common case, the original regex will be sandwiched between
117:         // two codepoints that are in the \W class. So our approach here is to
118:         // look for a match of the overall word regexp, strip the \W ends and
119:         // then check whether the original regex matches what's left. If so,
120:         // then we are guaranteed a correct match.
121:         //
122:         // This only works though if we know that the match is sandwiched
123:         // between two \W codepoints. This only occurs when neither ^ nor $
124:         // match. This in turn only occurs when the match is at either the
125:         // beginning or end of the haystack. In either of those cases, we
126:         // declare defeat and defer to the slower implementation.
127:         //
128:         // The reason why we cannot handle the ^/$ cases here is because we
129:         // can't assume anything about the original pattern. (Try commenting
130:         // out the checks for ^/$ below and run the tests to see examples.)
131:         let input = Input::new(haystack).span(at..haystack.len());
132:         let mut cand = match self.regex.find(input) {
133:             None => return Ok(None),
134:             Some(m) => Match::new(m.start(), m.end()),
135:         };
136:         if cand.start() == 0 || cand.end() == haystack.len() {
137:             return Err(());
138:         }
139:         let (_, slen) = bstr::decode_utf8(&haystack[cand]);
140:         let (_, elen) = bstr::decode_last_utf8(&haystack[cand]);
141:         let new_start = cand.start() + slen;
142:         let new_end = cand.end() - elen;
143:         // This occurs the original regex can match the empty string. In this
144:         // case, just bail instead of trying to get it right here since it's
145:         // likely a pathological case.
146:         if new_start > new_end {
147:             return Err(());
148:         }
149:         cand = cand.with_start(new_start).with_end(new_end);
150:         if self.original.is_match(&haystack[cand]) {
151:             Ok(Some(cand))
152:         } else {
153:             Err(())
154:         }
155:     }
156: }

158: impl Matcher for WordMatcher {
159:     type Captures = RegexCaptures;
160:     type Error = NoError;

162:     fn find_at(
163:         &self,
164:         haystack: &[u8],
165:         at: usize,
166:     ) -> Result<Option<Match>, NoError> {
167:         // To make this easy to get right, we extract captures here instead of
168:         // calling `find_at`. The actual match is at capture group `1` instead
169:         // of `0`. We *could* use `find_at` here and then trim the match after
170:         // the fact, but that's a bit harder to get right, and it's not clear
171:         // if it's worth it.
172:         //
173:         // OK, well, it turns out that it is worth it! But it is quite tricky.
174:         // See `fast_find` for details. Effectively, this lets us skip running
175:         // a slower regex engine to extract capture groups in the vast majority
176:         // of cases. However, the slower engine is I believe required for full
177:         // correctness.
178:         match self.fast_find(haystack, at) {
179:             Ok(Some(m)) => return Ok(Some(m)),
180:             Ok(None) => return Ok(None),
181:             Err(()) => {}
182:         }
183: 
184:         let input = Input::new(haystack).span(at..haystack.len());
185:         let mut caps = self.caps.get();
186:         self.regex.search_captures(&input, &mut caps);
187:         Ok(caps.get_group(1).map(|sp| Match::new(sp.start, sp.end)))
188:     }
189: 
190:     fn new_captures(&self) -> Result<RegexCaptures, NoError> {
191:         Ok(RegexCaptures::with_offset(self.regex.create_captures(), 1))
192:     }
193: 
194:     fn capture_count(&self) -> usize {
195:         self.regex.captures_len().checked_sub(1).unwrap()
196:     }
197: 
198:     fn capture_index(&self, name: &str) -> Option<usize> {
199:         self.names.get(name).map(|i| *i)
200:     }
201: 
202:     fn captures_at(
203:         &self,
204:         haystack: &[u8],
205:         at: usize,
206:         caps: &mut RegexCaptures,
207:     ) -> Result<bool, NoError> {
208:         let input = Input::new(haystack).span(at..haystack.len());
209:         let caps = caps.captures_mut();
210:         self.regex.search_captures(&input, caps);
211:         Ok(caps.is_match())
212:     }
213: 
214:     // We specifically do not implement other methods like find_iter or
215:     // captures_iter. Namely, the iter methods are guaranteed to be correct
216:     // by virtue of implementing find_at and captures_at above.
217: }

part.text:
Fixed `--word-regexp` incomplete matches in `crates/regex/src/word.rs`.

The issue came from an optimization that found the complete wrapper match and manually stripped surrounding `\W` characters. With greedy or ambiguous patterns, that could return a shorter but valid inner match such as `ome.domain.com`.

`WordMatcher::find_at` now always obtains the actual inner capture from the regex engine, matching the correct `-w` semantics while preserving existing wrapper behavior, including word matches that begin or end with non-word characters.

Validation:
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Attempted `cargo fmt --check` and `cargo test -p grep-regex word::tests` in the required container, but the container has neither `cargo` nor `rg` installed, so compilation/tests could not run.
- No tests were modified, and no changes were staged or committed.
